name: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare
title: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare
answer: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare is a structured review of how a care organisation selects, deploys and monitors artificial intelligence tools that touch patient care, clinical operations or billing. It sits inside governance, compliance and medical device security, and it borrows from software audit practice, regulatory inspection and clinical quality review. Its subject is not the model itself but the whole arrangement around it: the data it sees, the people who act on its output, the contracts that cover it and the evidence kept when something goes wrong. Because this site tracks 1,000 medical AI models, the audit has to cope with a crowded and fast changing vendor field rather than a handful of known products.

sections.body: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare is a structured review of how a care organisation selects, deploys and monitors artificial intelligence tools that touch patient care, clinical operations or billing. It sits inside governance, compliance and medical device security, and it borrows from software audit practice, regulatory inspection and clinical quality review. Its subject is not the model itself but the whole arrangement around it: the data it sees, the people who act on its output, the contracts that cover it and the evidence kept when something goes wrong. Because this site tracks 1,000 medical AI models, the audit has to cope with a crowded and fast changing vendor field rather than a handful of known products.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: An audit of this kind runs on the same systems the organisation already uses: the electronic health record, the model registry or inventory, the procurement and contract repository, the incident and complaint log, and the identity and access management stack. It also needs a way to capture model versions, training data provenance, validation results and post deployment performance in one place, because those records are usually scattered across vendors, IT and clinical departments. Cloud hosting arrangements matter here, since many clinical models are delivered as a service and the audit must establish where data is processed and stored. The output is typically a findings register with owners, dates and evidence links, not a single score.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by a small team, usually drawn from clinical informatics, compliance, security and the relevant clinical specialty, working against a written checklist or framework. They interview staff, walk through live workflows, inspect vendor documentation, test access controls, and sample real cases to see whether the model's output was reviewed by a qualified person before it changed care. Evidence is gathered as screenshots, extracts, meeting notes and signed attestations, then mapped to each control. Findings are rated by patient risk and by regulatory exposure, and the team agrees remediation steps with the responsible owner. Repeats are scheduled, because a model that passed at go live can drift once the patient mix or the upstream data changes.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on several overlapping duties: patient consent and notice, data protection, device regulation where the software qualifies as a medical device, and professional accountability for the clinician who acts on an output. Provenance is central, meaning the audit must be able to show which model version produced which output, on what data, and who reviewed it. Liability is no longer theoretical, and this site tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which is why documentation and audit trails are treated as core evidence rather than administrative overhead.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect the audit to move from periodic project review toward continuous monitoring, with automated logging of model versions, inputs and overrides feeding a standing register.Auditors will spend more time on drift, bias and post market surveillance, and less on one off pre purchase checks. The practical direction is a single evidence trail that satisfies clinical governance, security review and regulatory inspection at once, rather than three parallel exercises.
